title: Issue or risk? Telling them apart
blurb: Sort any event into risk or issue in seconds: uncertain and future, or certain and here now.
question: On a school extension, the head teacher warns that exam season might restrict noisy work in June, and the same week the crane hire firm collapses, leaving the site without a crane for five weeks, well past tolerance. Which is the risk, which is the issue, and why?

teach.body: A RISK is uncertain and lies in the future: it might happen, and if it does it will affect objectives, for better (an opportunity) or worse (a threat). An ISSUE is certain and here now: a problem that has happened and is breaching, or about to breach, delegated tolerances, so it is escalated to the sponsor. One line to remember: risks are 'might', issues are 'is'.

teach.h: What they share and what sets them apart
Risk and issue side by side
teach.caption: Both are written down and owned. The exam likes to claim only one of them needs recording: that is false.

teach.body: First: has it happened, or is it happening? If not, it is a risk. Second, if it has: does it breach, or is it about to breach, the delegated tolerances? If yes, it is an issue for the sponsor; if no, it is a day-to-day problem the project manager resolves. Watch the verbs in the scenario: 'may', 'could', 'might' point to risk; 'has', 'is', 'stopped' point to issue.

head: Event
Risk or issue?
Clue
rows: Grant may rise if energy target beaten
Exams may limit noisy work in June
teach.caption: Only problems that have happened can be issues. Opportunities are always risks.

teach.h: How a threat can become an issue

steps.label: Risk identified
steps.sub: Supplier might fail: in the register

teach.caption: The risk entry is closed as 'occurred' and the problem is managed as an issue.

teach.h: The link runs both ways, but not always
teach.body: A threat that materialises can become an issue. But not every issue was once on the risk register: some problems arrive out of the blue. And not every threat that occurs becomes an issue: if the PM can absorb it within tolerance, it is simply handled. Good risk management can mean fewer issues, but it can never guarantee none.

teach.text: Classic reversals: 'an issue is uncertain but a risk is not' is backwards, and 'an issue must be recorded but a risk need not be' is false: both are recorded. Also, an opportunity can never be an issue, because issues are problems.

items: Risk: uncertain, future, threat or opportunity, has a probability, managed proactively in the plan.
Issue: certain, here now, a problem breaching tolerances, escalated to the sponsor.
Both affect objectives, both are logged, owned and tracked to closure.
A threat that occurs can become an issue; an opportunity never can.

summary: You can now tell a risk from an issue on certainty, timing, direction and management, and sort a scenario quickly using the verbs it uses. You also know how a threat can turn into an issue, and why an opportunity never does.

A.q: Which statement correctly contrasts an issue with a risk?
options: An issue is certain and current; a risk is uncertain
An issue is uncertain and future; a risk is certain
An issue must be logged; a risk need not be recorded
An issue is always positive; a risk is always negative
A.why: An issue has happened (certain, now); a risk might happen (uncertain, future).

whyNot.1: This reverses the two: it is the risk that is uncertain.
whyNot.2: Both are recorded: risks in the risk register, issues in the issue log.
whyNot.3: Issues are problems, so never positive; risks can be threats or opportunities.

A.q: The team notes that a key subcontractor might go out of business next spring. This is best classified as:
options: an issue
a risk
an assumption
a dependency
A.why: It might happen in the future and would affect objectives, so it is a risk (a threat).

whyNot.0: Nothing has happened yet, so it is not an issue.
whyNot.2: An assumption is something taken to be true for planning; this is an uncertain event.
whyNot.3: A dependency is a link between activities or projects, not an uncertain event.

A.q: Which of these could only ever be a risk, never an issue?
options: A crane that broke down this morning
A budget overrun beyond tolerance
A permit refusal halting all work
A possible gain if a grant is approved
A.why: A possible gain is uncertain and positive: an opportunity. Issues are always problems that have happened.

whyNot.0: A breakdown that has happened is a current problem, so it can be an issue.
whyNot.1: An overrun past tolerance is a textbook issue.
whyNot.2: A refusal that has stopped the work is happening now, so it is an issue.

B.q: A cyber attack has just taken the project's booking system offline, and launch will now miss its time tolerance. How should it be classified?
options: A risk, as the size of its impact is not yet known
An issue, as it has happened and breaches tolerance
A risk, as a similar attack could happen again soon
An opportunity to rebuild the booking system properly
B.why: The attack has happened and the tolerance will be breached, so it is an issue for the sponsor.

whyNot.0: Uncertainty about the size of the impact doesn't make it a risk: the event itself has occurred.
whyNot.2: A repeat attack would be a separate risk; this attack is a current problem.
whyNot.3: This is a problem, not a positive uncertain event.

B.q: Which feature does a risk have that an issue does not?
options: A named owner
An impact
A probability
A log entry
B.why: A risk is uncertain, so it has a probability. An issue has already occurred.

whyNot.0: Both risks and issues have named owners.
whyNot.1: Both affect objectives, so both have an impact.
whyNot.3: Both are recorded: risk register and issue log.

B.q: A threat in the risk register occurs and breaches the time tolerance. How should it now be viewed?
options: It stays a risk, with a higher probability
It is closed, as nothing more can be done
It becomes a lesson for future projects only
It becomes an issue to escalate to the sponsor
B.why: Once a threat occurs and breaches tolerance it is no longer uncertain: it is managed as an issue and escalated.

whyNot.0: It has happened, so it is no longer uncertain and can't stay a risk.
whyNot.1: The risk entry is closed, but the problem itself must still be resolved.
whyNot.2: Lessons are captured, but the live problem must be managed now.

C.q:
Which TWO of the following are issues?
1. Rain is forecast that could flood the site next week.
2. The site has flooded and work beyond tolerance is lost.
3. A rival may launch a similar product first.
4. A regulator has refused the licence, halting the project.
options: 1 and 3
2 and 4
1 and 4
2 and 3
C.why: Statements 2 and 4 describe problems that have happened and are breaching tolerances.

whyNot.0: Both 1 and 3 are uncertain future events: risks.
whyNot.2: Statement 1 is a forecast that 'could' happen, so it is a risk.
whyNot.3: Statement 3 'may' happen, so it is a risk.

C.q: On the Northgate School project, the head says exams MAY restrict noisy work in June. Where should the project manager record this, and why?
options: Risk register: it is uncertain and future
Issue log: it involves the head teacher
Issue log: it would breach the schedule
Risk register: all school events go there
C.why: The restriction may or may not happen, and it is in the future, so it is a risk.

whyNot.1: Who raises a concern doesn't decide its type; certainty and timing do.
whyNot.2: It hasn't happened, so there is no current breach to log as an issue.
whyNot.3: Events go in the register because they are uncertain, not because they are school events.

C.q: Which statement about the link between risks and issues is correct?
options: Every issue started life on the risk register
A risk can never turn into an issue later on
A threat that occurs may become an issue
An issue that is resolved becomes a risk
C.why: When a threat materialises and breaches tolerance, it becomes an issue.

whyNot.0: Some issues arise without warning and were never identified as risks.
whyNot.1: Threats that occur can and do become issues.
whyNot.3: A resolved issue is closed; it doesn't turn back into a risk.

reteach.title: The festival control room
reteach.question: At a music festival, the organisers keep a 'what might happen' board and a 'what is happening' board. Which is the risk register and which is the issue log?

blocks.h: Two boards, two kinds of event
blocks.body: The 'might happen' board lists rain on Saturday, a ticket scanner failing, or a famous guest turning up and boosting sales: risks, good and bad. The 'is happening' board lists the headline act cancelling this afternoon: that is an issue, and the festival director (the sponsor) must agree the fix. When a 'might' comes true and is too big for the team, it moves boards.

items: 'Is' board = issues: problems happening now, beyond the team's limits.
A threat that comes true can move from one board to the other.

explain.body: A risk carries uncertainty: it may or may not happen. An issue carries none: it has happened or is happening.

test.q: Complete the statement: a risk is ______, whereas an issue is certain.
options: uncertain
urgent
escalated
negative
test.why: Uncertainty is the defining feature of a risk; an issue is certain.

whyNot.1: Urgency is not what separates them; issues are often the urgent ones.
whyNot.2: Escalation to the sponsor applies to issues, not risks.
whyNot.3: Risks can be positive opportunities as well as negative threats.

explain.body: A risk sits in the future. An issue sits in the present: it has occurred, or a breach is imminent. Listen for 'may', 'could', 'might' versus 'has', 'is', 'stopped'.

test.q: In terms of timing, which statement is true?
options: Risks lie in the past; issues lie in the future
Risks and issues both lie in the future
Risks are happening; issues may happen later
Risks may happen; issues are happening now
test.why: Risks are possible future events; issues are current problems.

whyNot.0: A risk is never in the past: once it has happened it is no longer a risk.

explain.body: Risks can be threats (negative) or opportunities (positive). Issues are always problems, so an opportunity can never be an issue.

test.q: Why can an opportunity never be an issue?
options: Opportunities are too small to need the sponsor
Issues are problems; opportunities are positive
Opportunities are always closed before they occur
Issues are only ever recorded by the sponsor
test.why: An issue is by definition a problem; an opportunity is an uncertain positive event, so it is a risk.

whyNot.0: Size is irrelevant; some opportunities are large.
whyNot.2: Opportunities can occur; the point is they are positive, not problems.
whyNot.3: The PM records issues in the issue log.

explain.body: Risks are managed proactively: assessed, given an owner and a planned response before they happen. Issues are managed now: logged, assessed and escalated to the sponsor to agree a resolution.

test.q: How does the management of a risk differ from that of an issue?
options: Risks go to the sponsor; issues stay with the team
Risks are logged once; issues are reviewed weekly
Risks are planned for ahead; issues are resolved now
Risks need change control; issues never alter plans
test.why: Risks get planned responses in advance; issues need resolving now, with the sponsor's support.

whyNot.0: It is issues that go to the sponsor, not risks.
whyNot.1: Risks are reviewed regularly too; the register is a living document.
whyNot.3: Issue resolutions can change the baseline, which is when change control applies.
